{{Short description|Inequality in information theory}}
In [[information theory]], '''Pinsker's inequality''', named after its inventor [[Mark Semenovich Pinsker]], is an [[inequality (mathematics)|inequality]] that bounds the [[total variation distance]] (or statistical distance) in terms of the [[Kullback–Leibler divergence]].
The inequality is tight up to constant factors.<ref>{{cite book|title=Information Theory: Coding Theorems for Discrete Memoryless Systems|first1=Imre|last1=Csiszár|first2=János|last2=Körner|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2011|isbn=9781139499989|page=44|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2gsLkQlb8JAC&pg=PA44}}</ref>

==Formal statement==
Pinsker's inequality states that, if <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math> are two [[probability distribution]]s on a [[measurable space]] <math>(X, \Sigma)</math>, then

:<math>\delta(P,Q) \le \sqrt{\frac{1}{2} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\parallel Q)},</math>

where

:<math>\delta(P,Q)=\sup \bigl\{ |P(A) - Q(A)| \mid \quad A \in \Sigma \text{ is a measurable event} \bigr\}</math>

is the [[Total variation distance of probability measures|total variation distance]] (or statistical distance) between <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math> and

:<math>D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\parallel Q) = \operatorname{E}_P \left( \log \frac{\mathrm{d} P}{\mathrm{d} Q} \right) = \int_X \left( \log \frac{\mathrm{d} P}{\mathrm{d} Q} \right) \, \mathrm{d} P</math>

is the [[Kullback–Leibler divergence]] in [[Nat (unit)|nats]].  When the sample space <math>X</math> is a [[finite set]], the Kullback–Leibler divergence is given by

: <math>D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\parallel Q) = \sum_{i \in X} \left( \log \frac{P(i)}{Q(i)}\right) P(i)\!</math>

Note that in terms of the [[Total_variation#Total_variation_of_a_measure|total variation norm]] <math>\| P - Q \|</math> of the [[signed measure]] <math>P - Q</math>, Pinsker's inequality differs from the one given above by a factor of two:
:<math>\| P - Q \| \le \sqrt{2 D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\parallel Q)}.</math>

A proof of Pinsker's inequality uses the [[partition inequality]] for [[f-divergence|''f''-divergences]].

=== Alternative version ===


Note that the expression of Pinsker inequality depends on what basis of [[logarithm]] is used in the definition of KL-divergence. <math>D_{KL}</math> is defined using <math>\ln</math> (logarithm in base <math>e</math>), whereas <math>D</math> is typically defined with <math>\log_2</math> (logarithm in base 2). Then,

:<math>D(P\parallel Q) =\frac{D_{KL}(P\parallel Q)}{\ln 2}.
</math>

Given the above comments, there is an alternative statement of Pinsker's inequality in some literature that relates [[Kullback–Leibler divergence|information divergence]] to variation distance: 
:<math>
  D(P\parallel Q) = \frac{D_{KL}(P\parallel Q)}{\ln 2} 
  \ge
  \frac{1}{2 \ln 2}
  V^2(p, q),
</math>
i.e.,
:<math>
  \sqrt{\frac{D_{KL}(P\parallel Q)}{2} }
  \ge
  \frac{V(p, q)}{2},
</math>
in which 
:<math>V(p, q) = 
  \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} 
  |p(x) - q(x) | 
</math>
is the [[total variation|(non-normalized) variation distance]] between two [[probability density function|probability density functions]] <math>p</math> and  <math>q</math> on the same alphabet <math>\mathcal{X}</math>.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Raymond W. |first1=Yeung |title=Information Theory and Network Coding |date=2008 |publisher=Springer |location=Hong Kong |isbn=978-0-387-79233-0 |page=26}}</ref>

This form of Pinsker's inequality shows that "convergence in divergence" is a stronger notion than "convergence in variation distance".

A simple proof by [[John_Pollard_(mathematician)|John Pollard]] is shown by letting <math>r(x)=P(x)/Q(x)-1 \ge -1</math>:
:<math>\begin{align}
  D_{KL}(P \parallel Q)
  &= E_Q[(1+r(x))\log(1+r(x))-r(x)]
  \\&\ge \frac{1}{2}E_Q\left[\frac{r(x)^2}{1+r(x)/3}\right]
  \\&\ge \frac{1}{2}\frac{E_Q[|r(x)|]^2}{E_Q[1+r(x)/3]}
&\text{(from Titu's lemma)}
  \\&= \frac{1}{2}E_Q[|r(x)|]^2
&\text{(As } E_Q[1+r(x)/3]=1 \text{ )}
  \\&= \frac{1}{2}V(p, q)^2.
\end{align}</math>
Here Titu's lemma is also known as [[Sedrakyan's inequality]].

Note that the lower bound from Pinsker's inequality is vacuous for any distributions where <math>D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\parallel Q)>2</math>, since the total variation distance is at most <math>1</math>. For such distributions, an alternative bound can be used, due to [[Bretagnolle–Huber inequality|Bretagnolle and Huber]]<ref>Bretagnolle, J.; Huber, C, ''Estimation des densités: risque minimax'', Séminaire de Probabilités, XII (Univ. Strasbourg, Strasbourg, 1976/1977), pp. 342–363, Lecture Notes in Math., 649, Springer, Berlin, 1978, Lemma 2.1 (French).</ref> (see, also, Tsybakov<ref>
Tsybakov, Alexandre B., ''Introduction to nonparametric estimation'', Revised and extended from the 2004 French original. Translated by Vladimir Zaiats. Springer Series in Statistics. Springer, New York, 2009. xii+214 pp. {{ISBN|978-0-387-79051-0}}, Equation 2.25.</ref>):
:<math>\delta(P,Q) \le \sqrt{1-e^{ -D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\parallel Q) }}.</math>

==History==
Pinsker first proved the inequality with a greater constant. The inequality in the above form was proved independently by [[Solomon Kullback|Kullback]], [[Imre Csiszár|Csiszár]], and [[Johannes Kemperman|Kemperman]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Tsybakov|first=Alexandre|title=Introduction to Nonparametric Estimation|url=https://archive.org/details/introductiontono00tsyb|url-access=limited|year=2009|publisher=Springer|isbn=9780387790527|page=[https://archive.org/details/introductiontono00tsyb/page/n142 132]}}</ref>

==Inverse problem==
A precise inverse of the inequality cannot hold:  for every <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>, there are distributions <math>P_\varepsilon, Q</math> with <math>\delta(P_\varepsilon,Q)\le\varepsilon</math> but <math>D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_\varepsilon\parallel Q) = \infty</math>. An easy example is given by the two-point space <math>\{0,1\}</math> with <math>Q(0) = 0, Q(1) = 1</math> and <math>P_\varepsilon(0) = \varepsilon, P_\varepsilon(1) = 1-\varepsilon</math>.<ref>The divergence becomes infinite whenever one of the two distributions assigns probability zero to an event while the other assigns it a nonzero probability (no matter how small); see e.g. {{cite book|title=Data Complexity in Pattern Recognition|first1=Mitra|last1=Basu|first2=Tin Kam|last2=Ho|publisher=Springer|year=2006|isbn=9781846281723|page=161|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GflBKbzym9oC&pg=PA161}}.</ref>

However, an inverse inequality holds on finite spaces <math>X</math> with a constant depending on <math>Q</math>.<ref>See Remark 1 in {{Cite book |last1=Sason |first1=Igal |last2=Verdú |first2=Sergio |chapter=Upper bounds on the relative entropy and Rényi divergence as a function of total variation distance for finite alphabets |year=2015 |title=2015 IEEE Information Theory Workshop - Fall (ITW) |pages=214–218 |doi=10.1109/ITWF.2015.7360766|arxiv=1503.03417 |isbn=978-1-4673-7852-9 }}</ref> More specifically, it can be shown that with the definition <math>\alpha_Q := \min_{x \in X: Q(x) > 0} Q(x)</math> we have for any measure <math>P</math> which is absolutely continuous to <math>Q</math>
: <math>\frac{1}{2} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\parallel Q) \le \frac{1}{\alpha_Q} \delta(P,Q)^2. </math>

As a consequence, if <math>Q</math> has full [[Support_(measure_theory)|support]] (i.e. <math>Q(x) > 0</math> for all <math>x \in X</math>), then

: <math> \delta(P,Q)^2 \le \frac{1}{2} D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\parallel Q) \le \frac{1}{\alpha_Q} \delta(P,Q)^2. </math>

== Proof of Pinsker’s inequality ==
'''Lemma 1.1 (Pinsker’s inequality) ''' ''Let'' <math>P</math> ''and'' <math>Q</math> ''be two distributions defined on the universe'' <math>U</math>. ''Then,'' <math>D(P||Q) \ge \frac{1}{2\ln2} \cdot || P-Q ||_1^2.</math><ref>Tulsiani, Madhur, and Gökalp Demirci. “I[https://home.ttic.edu/~madhurt/courses/infotheory2014/l5.pdf nformation and Coding Theory Lecture 5: October 14, 2014].” University of Chicago.</ref>

'''Proof:''' <u>A special case:</u>

<math>P = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{w.p. } p \\ 0, & \text{w.p. }1-p \end{cases}</math>

and, 

<math>Q = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{w.p. } q \\ 0, & \text{w.p. }1-q \end{cases}</math>

We assume <math>p \ge q</math> (other case is similar), and let 

<math>f(p,q) = p \log \frac{p}{q} + (1-p) \log \frac{1-p}{1-q} - \frac{1}{2 \ln 2}(2(p-q))^2.</math>

Since

<math>\frac{\partial f}{\partial q} = -\frac{p-q}{\ln 2} \left( \frac{1}{q(1-q)}-4 \right) \le 0,</math>

and <math>f=0</math> when <math>q=p</math>, we conclude that <math>f(p,q) \ge 0</math> where <math>q \le p.</math> Thus we have that <math>D(P||Q) \ge \tfrac{1}{2 \ln 2} || P-Q ||_1^2
 </math> for this special case.

<u>General case:</u> Let <math>P </math> and <math>Q </math> be distributions on <math>U. </math> Let <math>A \subset U </math> be

<math>A = \{x | p(x) \ge q(x) \}. </math>

and <math>P_A </math> and <math>Q_A </math> be

<math>P_A = \begin{cases} 
1, & \text{w.p. } \sum\limits_{x \in A} p(x) \\ 
0, & \text{w.p. } \sum\limits_{x \not\in A} p(x) 
\end{cases}
 </math>

<math>Q_A = \begin{cases} 
1, & \text{w.p. } \sum\limits_{x \in A} q(x) \\ 
0, & \text{w.p. } \sum\limits_{x \not\in A} q(x) 
\end{cases}
 </math>

Then,

<math>\begin{align}
||P-Q||_1 &= \sum\limits_{x} |p(x) - q(x)| \\
          &= \sum\limits_{x \in A} (p(x) - q(x)) + \sum\limits_{x \notin A} (q(x) - p(x)) \\
          &= \left| \sum\limits_{x \in A} p(x) - \sum\limits_{x \in A} q(x) \right| 
              + \left| \sum\limits_{x \notin A} p(x) - \sum\limits_{x \notin A} q(x) \right| \\
||P-Q||_1 &= ||P_A - Q_A||_1 &\text{(1)}
\end{align}


 </math>

Define a random variable <math>Z


 </math> as <math>Z = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } x\in A \\ 0, & \text{if }x \notin A \end{cases} .


 </math> We have that<math>D(P||Q) = D(P(Z)||Q(Z) ) + D(P||Q|Z).</math> Since <math>D( P(Z)||Q(Z)) = D(P_A || Q_A )</math> and <math>D(P||Q|Z) \ge0,</math> we have 

<math>\begin{align}
D(P||Q) &\ge D(P_A |\ Q_A) \\
        &\ge \frac{1}{2 \ln 2} \cdot ||P_A - Q_A|{|_1}^2 &\text{(use the special case)}\\
        &= \frac{1}{2 \ln 2} \cdot ||P - Q |{|_1}^2 &\text{(use equation 1)}
\end{align}
</math>
